body.text: 'Text me when you get home'. A pretend phone call on a low-lit street. Sharing your location before a first date.
These small acts of solidarity have long been commonplace in female friendships.
But as the public conversation around sexual violence and consent has grown, another kind of exchange has emerged: confiding about past sexual experiences that didn't feel right.
Experts say consent education has given women the language to name what happened to them, and many are finally gaining a sense of validation and justice years later.
A 'realisation' among friends
It's something writer and broadcaster Dee Salmin knows well.
"I've had multiple instances with friends where we're all having drinks and sharing some really vulnerable stories," Salmin says.
"That's where you start to have that reckoning and those realisations."
It was through these conversations that Salmin recognised her own teenage experience as sexual assault, years after it happened.
She says even though it "felt wrong" at the time, she internalised blame because she "froze" in the moment.
"I was gaslighting myself into thinking that I'd done something that told him it was OK," she says.
"It's only now in hindsight, with maturity and education that I see how messed up it was."
The consent void
Salmin believes a lack of consent education made her experience "almost inevitable" with her and her peers normalising unacceptable behaviour.
"If someone at that time had heard my story and been like, 'Oh, that's sexual assault,' that might have really changed the types of interactions I had with men," she says.
"Sex ed was literally just a condom on a banana."
It was only in her 20s, through her work on the sex and relationships podcast The Hook Up, that Salmin was able to understand and process her own sexual assault.
"I speak with so many incredible educators, activists and therapists and I now have such a strong understanding of consent and boundaries," she says.
When the realisation 'clicks'
Chanel Contos, founder and chief executive of Teach Us Consent, says someone might not identify a sexual assault in the moment because they're shocked, confused or don't have the words for it.
"It often clicks after learning about consent and what constitutes sexual violence," she says.
Ms Contos says this delayed realisation doesn't make the experience any less real or any less valid.
"In the moment, people might freeze, shut down or fawn ... that's a stress and survival response, not consent."
Because these responses aren't widely understood, Ms Contos says victim-survivors often carry the belief that they are at fault and tell themselves it was "just bad sex" or a "miscommunication".
"It is never their fault. Responsibility sits with the person who didn't seek or respect consent."
Why now?

Criminologist and social worker, Professor Anastasia Powell, says victim-survivors often knew their experience felt wrong, violating or frightening at the time, but it's only later that they fully recognised the harm.
Professor Powell, whose work focuses on sexual violence, says consent education in schools and increased media reporting have contributed to more awareness in the community.
"Recently we've seen extraordinary survivor advocates who have spoken openly about sexual violence and the failures of our institutions," she says.
"It can be common for someone to see these stories and recognise the parallels in their own life experience."
But Professor Powell says there are significant gaps in community knowledge with many people still having a "really narrow picture" of sexual violence.
"There is a really persistent stereotype ... that it's the stranger, it's very physically forced, that it's a victim who clearly says no and fights back," she says.
"In reality, sexual assault is very often committed by someone known to us, often a date or an intimate partner."

Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) data shows female victim-survivors knew the male perpetrator in 84 per cent of cases. It also shows that of those women who have been sexually assaulted, one in three of the incidents occurred in their own home.
Professor Powell says common scenarios can include being intoxicated or asleep, consenting to one act but not another, feeling pressured or intimidated or simply freezing.
Intentional language and labels
Labelling these experiences, where there is no active agreement or consent, helps the broader community understand what sexual assault actually is, according to Professor Powell.
"Naming that sexual violence really clearly is part of recognising its seriousness and holding perpetrators to account," she says.
However, Professor Powell acknowledges that words like rape and sexual assault can initially feel "very confronting".
"People do need to be able to find space to find the words for their own experience in their own time," she says.
In Salmin's case, she was reluctant to identify herself as a victim-survivor because she didn't want it to become a core part of her identity.
But she says sharing her story of sexual assault publicly was an important decision.
"It was really about being honest and naming things that a lot of women and girls experience that isn't spoken about as much as it should be," Salmin says.
The path to recovery
It's this sense of solidarity gained by exchanging "awful experiences" that Salmin has found to be "deeply bonding" and "healing".
"There's something really cathartic in realising you're not alone," she says.
"Lots of people won't want to talk about their experiences publicly or even privately to people, and that's absolutely fine.
"[But] if I can prevent someone from experiencing what I did, then [me speaking up] has been worth it."
Professor Powell says it's important for victim-survivors to be in control of their own story and to choose a pathway that feels right for them.
According to the ABS data, 92 per cent of women who experienced sexual assault by a male did not report the most recent incident to police.

Their reasons included: feeling like they could deal with it themselves, not regarding the incident as serious, feeling ashamed or embarrassed, thinking there was little the police could do, or feeling they wouldn't be believed.
"We know that criminal legal processes so often fail victim-survivors," she says.
"Justice doesn't have to mean a criminal prosecution. It might be more of a felt sense of justice that's much more personal."
This can come from having the support of friends, family or a counsellor, who believe you and recognise the harm, according to Professor Powell.
She says it is possible for victim-survivors to heal and recover, with some "having a stronger sense of themselves" over time.
"It's one experience, one of many different experiences we might have in our life. It doesn't have to define who we are as a person," she says.
